qa.q: If I can’t see God, how can I know he exists?
qa.a:
Every day we believe in many invisible things: wind, gravity, radio waves, love. We know them by their effects. The Bible says: “For the invisible things of him since the creation of the world are clearly seen, being perceived through the things that are made” (Romans 1:20).

The universe has a beginning and precise order; life carries complex information; the human heart has a moral sense and a longing for eternity. These are clues pointing to a Creator. They can’t “force” belief, but they make belief a reasonable choice.

Most importantly, God didn’t only leave clues—he came into the world himself in Jesus. If you want to know whether God exists and what he is like, the best way is to get to know Jesus.
qa.step: Spend ten quiet minutes outdoors this week observing nature. Write down one thing that amazes you and ask: is this an accident?
qa.tip: Don’t rush to “win” with arguments. Ask first: “Do you lean toward believing or not? Why?” There is often a personal story behind it.

refs.t: because that which is known of God is revealed in them, for God revealed it to them. For the invisible things of him since the creation of the world are clearly seen, being perceived through the things that are made, even his everlasting power and divinity, that they may be without excuse.
The heavens declare the glory of God. The expanse shows his handiwork.

qa.q: Don’t science and faith contradict each other?
qa.a:
Many great scientists were Christians: Newton, Kepler, Faraday, Mendel—and many outstanding scientists today have faith. They studied nature because they believed the universe was made by an orderly God and could therefore be understood.

Science answers “how it works”; faith answers “why it exists and what it means.” Analyzing the paint in a painting and knowing the painter’s intention are two different levels of question; one doesn’t replace the other.

The Bible isn’t a science textbook; it uses language people of its time could understand to show that God is Creator. Christians hold different views on some details (such as the timing of creation), but the core is shared: “In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth” (Genesis 1:1). The more science discovers the intricacy of the universe, the more it invites wonder at the Designer.
qa.step: Look up the faith story of a scientist you admire, or ask Xiaozhi: “Which scientists believed in God?”
qa.tip: It’s fine to admit you’re not a science expert. You can say, “That’s a good question—let’s look into it together.”

refs.t: In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth.
The heavens declare the glory of God. The expanse shows his handiwork. Day after day they pour out speech, and night after night they display knowledge.

qa.q: If God exists, why doesn’t he just show himself to me?
qa.a:
God has shown himself in many ways: in nature, in conscience, in history, and most clearly in Jesus. Jesus said, “He who has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9).

Yet when Jesus did miracles on earth, many still didn’t believe. Seeing doesn’t always lead to believing, because belief is often not only a matter of evidence but of the heart. God doesn’t want servants scared into obedience; he wants children who respond out of love.

God also promises: “You shall seek me and find me, when you search for me with all your heart” (Jeremiah 29:13). He often shows himself gently to those who seek: a verse that moves you, help that comes at the right time, an inexplicable peace. Seek him with a sincere heart, and you may find he is closer than you imagine.
qa.step: Each day this week say to God: “If you exist, let me know you.” Watch for responses in your daily life.
qa.tip: Share your own concrete experience of “sensing God”—it is more powerful than any argument.

refs.t: Jesus said to him, “Have I been with you such a long time, and do you not know me, Philip? He who has seen me has seen the Father. How do you say, ‘Show us the Father’?
You shall seek me and find me, when you search for me with all your heart.

qa.q: Humans evolved from apes—how could we be made by God?
qa.a:
Many people wonder this. First, Christians hold different views on how evolution and creation relate: some believe God created directly; others think God may have used a long process. But all Christians agree on a few core things: the universe and life are not accidents but God’s plan, and humans are made in God’s image with special dignity.

The Bible says “God created man in his own image” (Genesis 1:27), meaning humans can think, love, create, tell right from wrong, and have a relationship with God—things no animal has. However the body was formed, human worth and meaning come from the Creator.

Rather than getting stuck in debates over details, ask a more basic question: am I an accidental product, or a loved being? The answer shapes how you see yourself and your life.
qa.step: Read Psalm 139:13-16 and consider: if I was wonderfully made by God, how would I see myself?
qa.tip: Avoid debating scientific details. Bring the focus back to where human worth and meaning come from.

refs.t: God created man in his own image. In God’s image he created him; male and female he created them.
For you formed my inmost being. You knit me together in my mother’s womb. I will give thanks to you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made. Your works are wonderful. My soul knows that very well.

qa.q: There are so many gods—why only one God?
qa.a:
In Chinese communities we know many deities: the Earth God, Mazu, Guan Gong, Guanyin. Many began as historical figures or local guardians, each overseeing a place or a need. The God of the Bible is completely different: not one god among many, but the one who created heaven and earth and everything in it, including us.

The Bible says: “I am the LORD, and there is no one else. Besides me, there is no God” (Isaiah 45:5). This isn’t God’s arrogance but a statement of fact: as a building has one architect, the universe has one Creator.

And this one true God isn’t distant or frightening; he is love. He doesn’t need offerings to be appeased; instead, he paid the price himself to come and find us. Knowing this God isn’t adding one more deity, but returning to the true source of our life.
qa.step: Compare: what is the biggest difference between the deities you know and the God of the Bible who “comes looking for people”?
qa.tip: Respect their cultural background and don’t mock past beliefs. Explain using the distinction between Creator and created.

refs.t: I am the LORD, and there is no one else. Besides me, there is no God. I will strengthen you, though you have not known me,
This is eternal life, that they should know you, the only true God, and him whom you sent, Jesus Christ.

qa.q: I’ve tried praying, but I can’t feel God. What should I do?
qa.a:
Many sincere seekers have this experience. Not feeling doesn’t necessarily mean God isn’t there. On cloudy days the sun is still shining. Faith isn’t built on feelings but on God’s promises.

Sometimes God answers in ways we don’t expect: not a loud voice, but gradually growing peace, someone’s care, a passage suddenly becoming clear. When Elijah waited for God on the mountain, God wasn’t in the wind, the earthquake or the fire, but in “a still small voice” (1 Kings 19:12).

Try this: each day at a set time, read a short passage from a Gospel, say a sentence or two to God, and keep it up for thirty days, noting what you observe. Find a Christian friend to do it with you—God often answers people through people.
qa.step: Start a thirty-day experiment: read a passage of Mark each day, pray one sentence, write down one observation.
qa.tip: Don’t pressure them to “feel” something. Walk with them for a while and pray for them.

refs.t: He said, “Go out and stand on the mountain before the LORD.” Behold, the LORD passed by, and a great and strong wind tore the mountains and broke in pieces the rocks before the LORD; but the LORD was not in the wind. After the wind there was an earthquake; but the LORD was not in the earthquake. After the earthquake a fire passed; but the LORD was not in the fire. After the fire, there was a still small voice.
You shall seek me and find me, when you search for me with all your heart.

qa.q: If God is love, why is there so much suffering in the world?
qa.a:
This is humanity’s oldest and most painful question, and the Bible doesn’t avoid it. Job, David and Jeremiah all cried out to God: why?

The Bible tells us several things. First, the source of suffering isn’t God; after people turned from God, the whole world entered brokenness. Much suffering is caused by human sin (war, oppression, violence), and some happens in a broken world (disease, disasters). Second, God hasn’t stood by; he entered human suffering himself: Jesus was betrayed, whipped and crucified. God isn’t watching us suffer from afar; he suffers with us. Third, suffering isn’t the final word. God promises a day when “He will wipe away every tear from their eyes. Death will be no more; neither will there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain any more” (Revelation 21:4).

We may not understand the reason for every suffering, but we can know the God who is with us in it.
qa.step: If you are suffering, tell God honestly, as the psalm writers did. You may weep and you may ask.
qa.tip: For someone who is suffering, be present and weep with them first; don’t rush to explain. Job’s friends were at their best when they sat with him seven days without a word.

refs.t: He will wipe away every tear from their eyes. Death will be no more; neither will there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain any more. The first things have passed away.”
For I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which will be revealed toward us.

qa.q: Something terrible happened to me. Is God punishing me?
qa.a:
Many people think this when misfortune strikes, especially those shaped by ideas of karma. Jesus’ disciples asked something similar about a man born blind: “Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?” Jesus answered: “This man didn’t sin, nor did his parents, but that the works of God might be revealed in him” (John 9:2-3).

Not every misfortune is punishment. The Bible has many examples of righteous people suffering; Jesus himself suffered. For those who believe in Jesus, the punishment for sin has already been borne by Jesus on the cross. God does sometimes discipline us, but discipline comes from a father’s love and aims at our growth, not revenge.

What you may need most right now isn’t an answer but to know you aren’t alone. God hasn’t left you; he says, “I will in no way leave you, neither will I in any way forsake you” (Hebrews 13:5).
qa.step: Write down your deepest pain and tell God—and one person you trust.
qa.tip: If they are in serious trauma or emotional crisis, encourage professional help. If thoughts of self-harm appear, gently but immediately help them connect with professional resources and trusted people.

refs.t: As he passed by, he saw a man blind from birth. His disciples asked him, “Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?” Jesus answered, “This man didn’t sin, nor did his parents, but that the works of God might be revealed in him.
Be free from the love of money, content with such things as you have, for he has said, “I will in no way leave you, neither will I in any way forsake you.”

qa.q: Why do good people suffer while bad people prosper?
qa.a:
Three thousand years ago, the psalmist Asaph wrestled with the same thing: “For I was envious of the arrogant, when I saw the prosperity of the wicked” (Psalm 73:3). He saw the wicked rich, healthy and proud, while he lived uprightly and suffered—and he nearly lost his faith.

The turning point came “until I entered God’s sanctuary, and considered their latter end” (Psalm 73:17). Seeing from eternity’s perspective, he understood: this life isn’t the whole story. God is just and will judge everything in the end. What looks unfair today isn’t unknown to God; he is waiting, giving people time to repent.

And for those who trust God, the greatest treasure isn’t an easy life but God himself. Asaph ends: “Whom do I have in heaven? There is no one on earth whom I desire besides you” (Psalm 73:25).
qa.step: Read Psalm 73 and watch how Asaph moves from resentment to peace.
qa.tip: Affirm that their sense of injustice is real, and walk with them from a temporary to an eternal perspective.

refs.t: For I was envious of the arrogant, when I saw the prosperity of the wicked.
When I tried to understand this, it was too painful for me— until I entered God’s sanctuary, and considered their latter end.
Whom do I have in heaven? There is no one on earth whom I desire besides you. My flesh and my heart fails, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever.

qa.q: I prayed for God to heal my loved one, but they died. Why didn’t God listen?
qa.a:
Losing someone you love is deep pain, especially after praying earnestly. First, allow yourself to grieve. At Lazarus’ tomb, “Jesus wept” (John 11:35). God won’t blame you for your tears or your questions.

God heard the prayer, but his answer isn’t always what we asked. We see one part of this life; God sees all of eternity. For those who believe in Jesus, death isn’t the end but going home to the Father. Jesus said: “I am the resurrection and the life. He who believes in me will still live, even if he dies” (John 11:25).

You don’t have to pretend to be strong or understand right away. You can come to God with sorrow—even anger. Many people experience God’s deepest comfort in grief. If grief disrupts your life for a long time, please also seek grief counseling or professional help.
qa.step: Write a letter to the loved one who has gone, and a letter to God, saying everything in your heart.
qa.tip: Don’t use “It was God’s will” to cut their grief short. Be present, listen, and remember to check in on anniversaries.

refs.t: Jesus said to her, “I am the resurrection and the life. He who believes in me will still live, even if he dies. Whoever lives and believes in me will never die. Do you believe this?”
Jesus wept.
The LORD is near to those who have a broken heart, and saves those who have a crushed spirit.

qa.q: Why does God allow bad things to happen to children and innocent people?
qa.a:
This is the most heartbreaking question, and honestly no answer fully resolves it. What we can say is that God hates evil—more than we do. Jesus said: “whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it would be better for him if a huge millstone were hung around his neck and that he were sunk in the depths of the sea” (Matthew 18:6). God treasures every child and every innocent person.

God gave people real freedom, and people often use it to harm others. God doesn’t forcibly cancel human freedom, but he will never let evildoers escape; all will give account before him. At the same time, God calls his people to stand beside the suffering: protecting the vulnerable, speaking up for the innocent, comforting the wounded.

If you or someone you know is being harmed, please don’t bear it alone. Make sure of safety first and seek trusted adults, professional agencies or the police. That too is God’s heart.
qa.step: Is there someone near you who needs protection or comfort? What could you do for them?
qa.tip: If the person is a victim, prioritize safety and professional help; don’t urge them to “forgive quickly” or “submit.”

refs.t: but whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it would be better for him if a huge millstone were hung around his neck and that he were sunk in the depths of the sea.

LORD, you have heard the desire of the humble. You will prepare their heart. You will cause your ear to hear, to judge the fatherless and the oppressed, that man who is of the earth may terrify no more.

qa.q: Will life be smooth sailing once I believe in Jesus?
qa.a:
No. This is important and needs to be said honestly. Jesus said: “In the world you have trouble; but cheer up! I have overcome the world” (John 16:33). Believing in Jesus isn’t buying “life insurance” against illness, job loss or hardship.

What believing changes is that in suffering we have God’s presence, hope and meaning. In the same storm, one boat has no anchor and another has dropped anchor; the waves are equally big, but the outcomes differ.

Some think believing will make them rich and everything will go well, and when trouble comes they leave disappointed. True faith isn’t “God will give me what I want,” but “whatever happens, God is with me, and he is good.” That kind of faith can weather life’s storms.
qa.step: Read Isaiah 43:2. Write down your current “waters” and “fires,” and beside them write: God is with me.
qa.tip: Avoid prosperity-gospel promises. Share your own real story of God’s presence in hardship.

refs.t: I have told you these things, that in me you may have peace. In the world you have trouble; but cheer up! I have overcome the world.”
When you pass through the waters, I will be with you, and through the rivers, they will not overflow you. When you walk through the fire, you will not be burned, and flame will not scorch you.

qa.q: Did Jesus really exist, or is he just a legend?
qa.a:
The vast majority of historians—including non-believing scholars—agree that Jesus was a real historical person. Besides the New Testament, first- and second-century non-Christian writers such as the Roman historian Tacitus and the Jewish historian Josephus mention Jesus and his crucifixion.

The four Gospels were written within decades of Jesus’ death, while many eyewitnesses were still alive. Luke says he wrote after “having traced the course of all things accurately from the first” (Luke 1:3). And New Testament manuscripts far outnumber those of any other ancient document.

So the real question isn’t “Did Jesus exist?” but “Who is Jesus?” Was he just a good teacher, or truly who he said he was—the Son of God and Savior of the world?
qa.step: Read Mark 1–2 and see what kind of person Jesus is.
qa.tip: You can recommend concise apologetics resources, but bring the focus to the personal question: “Who do you say Jesus is?”

refs.t: Since many have undertaken to set in order a narrative concerning those matters which have been fulfilled among us, even as those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and servants of the word delivered them to us, it seemed good to me also, having traced the course of all things accurately from the first, to write to you in order, most excellent Theophilus; that you might know the certainty concerning the things in which you were instructed.

That which was from the beginning, that which we have heard, that which we have seen with our eyes, that which we saw, and our hands touched, concerning the Word of life (and the life was revealed, and we have seen, and testify, and declare to you the life, the eternal life, which was with the Father, and was revealed to us); that which we have seen and heard we declare to you, that you also may have fellowship with us. Yes, and our fellowship is with the Father and with his Son, Jesus Christ.

qa.q: Jesus was a great teacher—why say he is God?
qa.a:
Many respect Jesus and place him alongside Confucius and the Buddha as great sages. But Jesus’ own words make it hard to treat him merely as a teacher. He said, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). He forgave sins, accepted worship, and said he is “the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6).

C. S. Lewis pointed out that someone who said such things, if they weren’t true, would be either a liar or a lunatic; but Jesus’ words and deeds show he was neither. The remaining possibility is that he really is who he said.

More importantly, Jesus rose from the dead, confirming his claims. A teacher can show you how to walk; Jesus says he is the way. A teacher can point out the problem; Jesus solved it himself.
qa.step: Read John chapter 1 and notice how John introduces Jesus.
qa.tip: Respect their regard for other sages, while gently pointing out that Jesus’ claims are unique.

refs.t: I and the Father are one.”
Jesus said to him, “I am the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father, except through me.
Thomas answered him, “My Lord and my God!”

qa.q: How can a dead person come back to life?
qa.a:
If there is no God, a resurrection is impossible. But if there is a God who created life, raising the dead isn’t hard for him. The key question is: is there enough evidence that Jesus really rose?

Several historical facts are hard to explain otherwise. First, the empty tomb: opponents couldn’t produce Jesus’ body. Second, many people saw the risen Jesus at different times and places; Paul says he once appeared to more than five hundred, “most of whom remain until now” (1 Corinthians 15:6). Third, the disciples went from fleeing in fear to proclaiming boldly, even to martyrdom—people don’t die for a lie they made up. Fourth, Christianity rapidly arose in the very city where Jesus was crucified.

The resurrection is the foundation of Christian faith. Paul says, “If Christ has not been raised, your faith is vain” (1 Corinthians 15:17). Because it matters so much, it deserves serious investigation.
qa.step: List your reasons “for” and “against” believing Jesus rose, and discuss them with the person walking with you.
qa.tip: Encourage honest inquiry, while sharing that final certainty often comes from meeting the risen Lord.

Then he appeared to over five hundred brothers at once, most of whom remain until now, but some have also fallen asleep. Then he appeared to James, then to all the apostles, and last of all, as to the child born at the wrong time, he appeared to me also.
If Christ has not been raised, your faith is vain; you are still in your sins.

qa.q: The Bible was written by people—how can it be God’s word? Hasn’t it been changed?
qa.a:
The Bible was indeed written by people—about forty authors over 1,500 years. But it claims these authors were moved by God: “For no prophecy ever came by the will of man, but holy men of God spoke, being moved by the Holy Spirit” (2 Peter 1:21). Like a pen in a writer’s hand: the pen is the tool, the meaning comes from the writer.

As for changes: there are more than five thousand Greek manuscripts of the New Testament, plus many early translations and quotations, which scholars can compare to reconstruct the original text quite accurately. The Dead Sea Scrolls, discovered in 1947, gave us Old Testament manuscripts a thousand years older than those previously known, and their content closely matches later copies. Manuscripts do differ in small ways (mostly spelling and word order), but none affects the core teachings of the Christian faith.

The Bible’s greatest evidence is its power to change lives. You can read it for yourself.
qa.step: Choose a Gospel and read it for seven days in a row, writing down the sentences that speak to you.
qa.tip: You don’t have to be an archaeologist to answer. Research together, and share how the Bible has changed you.

refs.t: knowing this first, that no prophecy of Scripture is of private interpretation. For no prophecy ever came by the will of man, but holy men of God spoke, being moved by the Holy Spirit.

Every Scripture is God-breathed and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for instruction in righteousness, that each person who belongs to God may be complete, thoroughly equipped for every good work.

qa.q: Some parts of the Bible seem to contradict each other. How do you explain that?
qa.a:
When reading the Bible we sometimes find things that look inconsistent—for example, the four Gospels give different details of the same event. That is actually normal: four witnesses wrote from different angles for different readers, like four reporters covering the same game, each emphasizing different points without anyone lying. If the four Gospels were identical, we’d suspect collusion.

Many so-called “contradictions” have reasonable explanations once we understand the language, culture and writing customs of the time. Some passages remain hard and scholars still study them, but none affects the core message: God loves the world, and Jesus died and rose for sinners.

When you find something you don’t understand, write it down and ask the person walking with you, ask Xiaozhi, or check a reliable reference. God isn’t afraid of our questions; honest inquiry often leads to deeper understanding.
qa.step: Write down passages that seem contradictory to you, and study them with the person walking with you.
qa.tip: Honestly admit some difficulties; don’t give glib answers. You can say, “I don’t know either—let’s find out together.”

refs.t: Since many have undertaken to set in order a narrative concerning those matters which have been fulfilled among us, even as those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and servants of the word delivered them to us, it seemed good to me also, having traced the course of all things accurately from the first, to write to you in order, most excellent Theophilus; that you might know the certainty concerning the things in which you were instructed.
Open my eyes, that I may see wondrous things out of your law.

qa.q: Why is Jesus the only way? Isn’t that narrow-minded?
qa.a:
This is one of the most common modern questions. “Only” sounds exclusive. But note: Christians didn’t invent this; Jesus himself said it: “I am the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father, except through me” (John 14:6).

If people could reach God through their own effort, practice or good works, Jesus wouldn’t have needed to go to the cross. Precisely because people can’t do it themselves, God prepared a way himself. Someone at the bottom of a deep well doesn’t need more climbing techniques; they need someone above to lower a rope.

And this way is open to everyone—any race, status or past: “Whoever will call on the name of the Lord will be saved” (Romans 10:13). It is the widest in whom it welcomes, and unique only in how. Christians say this not out of pride, but as beggars who were fed, telling other beggars where to find bread.
qa.step: Consider: if people could reach God on their own, why would Jesus need to die?
qa.tip: Explain humbly and avoid criticizing other religions. Stress that the gospel is grace, not Christians being better than others.

refs.t: Jesus said to him, “I am the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father, except through me.
There is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven that is given among men, by which we must be saved!”
For, “Whoever will call on the name of the Lord will be saved.”

qa.q: Don’t all religions teach people to be good? Isn’t it all the same?
qa.a:
Many religions do teach people to do good, and that deserves respect. But looking closely, religions answer the deepest questions very differently: Who is God? What is the human problem? How are we saved? Where do we go after death? These answers can’t all be true at once.

Most religions take the route of human effort: practice and good deeds to reach some state. The Christian faith says people can’t do it, so God came himself to save them. It’s a fundamental difference—not “people climbing up,” but “God coming down.” “For by grace you have been saved through faith, and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God, not of works, that no one would boast” (Ephesians 2:8-9).

So Christian faith isn’t only “teaching people to be good” but “giving people new birth”: God gives new life, and good works flow naturally from it. You can compare honestly and ask: which answer best meets the real need of my heart?
qa.step: Write down your view of “how people are saved,” then compare it with Ephesians 2:8-9.
qa.tip: Don’t belittle their religious background. Affirm the good in it, then explain what is unique about the gospel.

refs.t: for by grace you have been saved through faith, and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God, not of works, that no one would boast.
Jesus said to him, “I am the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father, except through me.

qa.q: My family practices folk worship (incense, ancestor rites). What should I do after believing in Jesus?
qa.a:
This is the most common difficulty for Chinese seekers, and it calls for wisdom and gentleness. Christians don’t worship idols or ancestor tablets, because worship belongs only to the God who made heaven and earth (Exodus 20:3-5). But that doesn’t mean not loving family or not remembering ancestors.

Some practical suggestions: First, explain respectfully; don’t criticize your family’s beliefs or damage the family altar. Second, during rites you can stand respectfully nearby and thank God in your heart for your ancestors, without holding incense or bowing. Third, express filial love in other ways, even more than before: help prepare the offerings, clean the graves at memorial times, tell your ancestors’ stories, care more attentively for elders. Fourth, if you are head of the household and decide to remove idols from the home, it is best to have your pastor and church family pray and handle it with you, with family agreement.

Most importantly, let your family see that those who believe in Jesus are more filial and love their family more. That is more powerful than any explanation.
qa.step: Discuss with the person walking with you: at the next family rite, how can I honor my faith while showing respect for my family?
qa.tip: Don’t push them into conflict with family. Help them plan concrete steps and pray for their family together. If conflict is severe, bring a pastor alongside.

refs.t: “You shall have no other gods before me. “You shall not make for yourselves an idol, nor any image of anything that is in the heavens above, or that is on the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth: you shall not bow yourself down to them, nor serve them, for I, the LORD your God, am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children, on the third and on the fourth generation of those who hate me,
“Honor your father and mother,” which is the first commandment with a promise: “that it may be well with you, and you may live long on the earth.”

But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts. Always be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you a reason concerning the hope that is in you, with humility and fear, having a good conscience. Thus, while you are spoken against as evildoers, they may be disappointed who curse your good way of life in Christ.

qa.q: After believing, can’t I hold incense or eat food that was offered?
qa.a:
Holding incense and bowing are acts of worship, which Christians avoid because worship belongs to God alone. But being present, standing respectfully and helping with chores are all fine—and are ways to show love and respect.

About eating food that was offered, the Bible discusses this in 1 Corinthians 8 and 10: food itself isn’t the issue, for “the earth is the Lord’s, and its fullness” (1 Corinthians 10:26). But if eating would make people think you are joining in idol worship, or your own conscience is uneasy, you may politely decline. Paul’s principle: don’t let your freedom cause others to stumble; do everything for God’s glory.

Different churches may give different guidance on details; ask your pastor or spiritual parent. The principle: be clear in your heart that you worship only God, and act toward your family with love and wisdom.
qa.step: Read 1 Corinthians 10:31 and consider: in family settings, how can I “do all to the glory of God”?
qa.tip: Avoid turning faith into a list of taboos. Help them understand the principles: worship belongs to God alone; do everything in love.

refs.t: Whatever is sold in the butcher shop, eat, asking no question for the sake of conscience, for “the earth is the Lord’s, and its fullness.” But if one of those who don’t believe invites you to a meal, and you are inclined to go, eat whatever is set before you, asking no questions for the sake of conscience. But if anyone says to you, “This was offered to idols,” don’t eat it for the sake of the one who told you, and for the sake of conscience. For “the earth is the Lord’s, with all its fullness.” Conscience, I say, not your own, but the other’s conscience. For why is my liberty judged by another conscience? If I partake with thankfulness, why am I denounced for something I give thanks for? Whether therefore you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God.

But food will not commend us to God. For neither, if we don’t eat are we the worse, nor if we eat are we the better. But be careful that by no means does this liberty of yours become a stumbling block to the weak.

qa.q: How do Christians observe Qingming (Tomb-Sweeping Day) and the Ghost Festival?
qa.a:
Qingming is a festival for remembering ancestors and expressing filial love, and Christians can observe it well: visiting and cleaning graves, bringing flowers, sharing ancestors’ stories with family, thanking God for their kindness. These are beautiful expressions of filial love and don’t conflict with faith. Many churches also hold memorial services around Qingming.

The Ghost Festival rites mainly involve offerings to wandering spirits, which differ from Christian beliefs. Christians believe the dead are in God’s hands and need no offerings from the living, and we need not fear. You can decline to take part in the offerings while explaining gently to family and neighbors, and help with other tasks if needed.

Festivals are good opportunities to show love to family: come home more readily and spend time with elders more attentively. Let your family see that believing in Jesus doesn’t mean abandoning ancestors, but remembering them with truer love.
qa.step: For this Qingming (or the next family gathering), plan one concrete act of filial love.
qa.tip: Help them decide what to do before the festival to avoid on-the-spot conflict; invite them to a church memorial service.

refs.t: “Honor your father and your mother, that your days may be long in the land which the LORD your God gives you.
For he will never be shaken. The righteous will be remembered forever.

qa.q: What’s wrong with fortune-telling, feng shui, or praying at temples for safety?
qa.a:
Many people seek fortune-telling and feng shui because they feel uneasy about the future and want something to lean on. That unease is understandable. But the Bible warns against divination and consulting spirits (Deuteronomy 18:10-12), because it entrusts our life to powers other than God, and it often leaves people living in more fear: fear of clashing dates, wrong directions, unlucky days.

Christian faith offers a different security: not mastering the secrets of fate, but knowing the one who governs it. Jesus said: “Therefore don’t be anxious for tomorrow, for tomorrow will be anxious for itself. Each day’s own evil is sufficient” (Matthew 6:34). He also said the hairs of our head are numbered, and not one sparrow falls without the Father.

After believing in Jesus, you can bring your desire for safety straight to the Father in prayer; he is our shepherd. This isn’t losing protection but gaining greater protection and true freedom.
qa.step: Write down your biggest worry about the future, pray through Psalm 23, and hand it to God.
qa.tip: Understand the unease and need behind it rather than simply forbidding. Help them experience the peace that prayer brings.

refs.t: There shall not be found with you anyone who makes his son or his daughter to pass through the fire, one who uses divination, one who tells fortunes, or an enchanter, or a sorcerer, or a charmer, or someone who consults with a familiar spirit, or a wizard, or a necromancer. For whoever does these things is an abomination to the LORD. Because of these abominations, the LORD your God drives them out from before you.
Therefore don’t be anxious for tomorrow, for tomorrow will be anxious for itself. Each day’s own evil is sufficient.

The LORD is my shepherd; I shall lack nothing. He makes me lie down in green pastures. He leads me beside still waters. He restores my soul. He guides me in the paths of righteousness for his name’s sake. Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for you are with me. Your rod and your staff, they comfort me.

qa.q: My Buddhist/Taoist friend is a good person. What happens if they don’t believe in Jesus?
qa.a:
Your friend may be very kind and cultivated, which deserves respect. The Bible never says only Christians do good. But it also says salvation isn’t by good works but by God’s grace. Just as we weren’t saved because we were good enough, others aren’t lost because they weren’t good enough; everyone equally needs grace.

How God will finally judge each person is in God’s hands. We know God is just and loving, “not wishing that anyone should perish, but that all should come to repentance” (2 Peter 3:9). We don’t need to sit in the judge’s seat over others.

What we can do is love your friend, pray for them, and when the time is right, gently share your own experience. Many people aren’t argued into faith but moved by love. Perhaps one day you will be the bridge by which they come to know Jesus.
qa.step: Pray for this friend for a week, and look for a chance to care sincerely for their needs.
qa.tip: Avoid making them feel Christians are judging others. Emphasize grace and humility, and encourage them to be a blessing to their friend.

refs.t: The Lord is not slow concerning his promise, as some count slowness; but he is patient with us, not wishing that anyone should perish, but that all should come to repentance.
for by grace you have been saved through faith, and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God, not of works, that no one would boast.

qa.q: I’m a good person and haven’t killed anyone. Why say I’m a sinner?
qa.a:
In the Bible, “sin” isn’t only breaking laws but “missing the mark”: not living as God made us to, centering life on ourselves instead of God. Jesus said the greatest commandment is “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind,” and the second, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matthew 22:37-39). Measured by that standard, no one succeeds.

Compared with other people we may seem fine, but by God’s standard “all have sinned, and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23). It’s like swimming across the Pacific: one person swims a hundred meters, another ten kilometers, but no one reaches the other side. The difference isn’t who swims farther; we all need a boat.

It’s natural to feel uncomfortable hearing you are a “sinner.” But the diagnosis is for healing. Because we all need it, Jesus came; and because grace is for sinners, everyone can receive it.
qa.step: Use Matthew 22:37-39 as a mirror and honestly write down what you see.
qa.tip: Share your own sin and brokenness so they don’t feel accused. Emphasize “we all are.”

refs.t: for all have sinned, and fall short of the glory of God;

Jesus said to him, “‘You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind.’ This is the first and great commandment. A second likewise is this, ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’
All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all.

qa.q: I’ve done terrible things. Will God really forgive me?
qa.a:
Yes. The Bible is full of people who did terrible things and were forgiven: David committed adultery and murder; Peter denied the Lord three times; Paul persecuted and killed Christians. Paul wrote that “Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am chief” (1 Timothy 1:15). If God could forgive him, he can forgive you.

God’s forgiveness doesn’t depend on how great the sin is but on how great the price Jesus paid. Jesus’ blood is enough to cleanse every sin: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9).

After forgiveness, some consequences may still need facing (such as apologizing or taking responsibility), but you are no longer condemned. You can lift your head and begin a new life. If the matter involves others who were harmed or legal issues, please consult a pastor or professional about how to take responsibility well.
qa.step: Tell God about it specifically and receive his forgiveness; if needed, pray with a trusted mature believer.
qa.tip: Keep confidence and respect; don’t show shock or judgment. Help them rest their assurance on God’s promise.

refs.t: If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
The saying is faithful and worthy of all acceptance, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am chief.
“Come now, and let’s reason together,” says the LORD: “Though your sins are as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow. Though they are red like crimson, they shall be as wool.

qa.q: If believing in Jesus saves me, can’t I just sin as I like?
qa.a:
Paul was asked the same question: “Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound?” His answer was direct: “May it never be! We who died to sin, how could we live in it any longer?” (Romans 6:1-2).

Someone truly touched by grace doesn’t want to keep hurting the God who loves them. A deeply loved and forgiven child doesn’t deliberately break their parents’ hearts again and again. Grace isn’t a license for indulgence but power for change. God doesn’t only forgive us; he gives new life and the Holy Spirit, so we gradually come to hate sin and love what is right.

Of course, believers still stumble, but they grieve, confess and want to change. If someone claims to believe in Jesus yet doesn’t care about sin at all, it may be worth asking: have I truly met this God of grace?
qa.step: Consider: how has being loved and forgiven changed your attitude toward sin?
qa.tip: Explain how grace and growth fit together: grace is both the starting point and the ongoing power for change.

refs.t: What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? May it never be! We who died to sin, how could we live in it any longer? Or don’t you know that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? We were buried therefore with him through baptism into death, that just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we also might walk in newness of life.

For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to all men, instructing us to the intent that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we would live soberly, righteously, and godly in this present age;

qa.q: What about people who have never heard the gospel?
qa.a:
This is a very loving question. The Bible tells us God is perfectly just, and he judges each person by truth and the light they have (Romans 2:11-16). God won’t be unfair. The Bible also says salvation is only through Jesus (Acts 4:12). How God deals with those who never heard the gospel isn’t spelled out in detail; we can trust his justice and love.

But the Bible is clear about one thing: for us, this question means mission. Precisely because some haven’t heard, Jesus commanded: “Go into all the world and preach the Good News to the whole creation” (Mark 16:15).

So more important than worrying about others are two things: first, you have heard—how will you respond? Second, will you tell those around you who haven’t heard?
qa.step: Think of someone near you who hasn’t heard the gospel, and pray for them.
qa.tip: Acknowledge that Christians hold different theological views; avoid being overly dogmatic, and bring the focus back to personal response and mission.

refs.t: For there is no partiality with God. For as many as have sinned without the law will also perish without the law. As many as have sinned under the law will be judged by the law. For it isn’t the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law will be justified (for when Gentiles who don’t have the law do by nature the things of the law, these, not having the law, are a law to themselves, in that they show the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience testifying with them, and their thoughts among themselves accusing or else excusing them) in the day when God will judge the secrets of men, according to my Good News, by Jesus Christ.
There is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven that is given among men, by which we must be saved!”
He said to them, “Go into all the world and preach the Good News to the whole creation.

qa.q: Is hell real? How could a loving God send people there?
qa.a:
Jesus spoke about hell more than about heaven, because he didn’t want anyone to go there. The Bible describes hell as eternal separation from God. God is the source of life, light and love; to be apart from God is to be apart from all of these.

Hell isn’t God enjoying punishment but God respecting human choice. Someone who says all their life “I don’t want God” is finally granted that—forever without God. C. S. Lewis put it this way: in the end there are only two kinds of people—those who say to God, “Thy will be done,” and those to whom God says, “Thy will be done.”

To keep people from perishing, God paid the greatest price: “For God so loved the world, that he gave his only born Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life” (John 3:16). The reality of hell shows how deep the love of the cross is.
qa.step: Read John 3:16-18 and notice whether God’s intention is to “save” or to “condemn.”
qa.tip: Speak gently and sincerely; don’t use fear tactics. Emphasize that God’s heart is to save.

refs.t: For God so loved the world, that he gave his only born Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life. For God didn’t send his Son into the world to judge the world, but that the world should be saved through him. He who believes in him is not judged. He who doesn’t believe has been judged already, because he has not believed in the name of the only born Son of God.
The Lord is not slow concerning his promise, as some count slowness; but he is patient with us, not wishing that anyone should perish, but that all should come to repentance.

qa.q: Can someone be saved by believing at the very end? Then can I believe later?
qa.a:
Yes. The thief beside the cross turned to Jesus just before dying, and Jesus said, “Assuredly I tell you, today you will be with me in Paradise” (Luke 23:43). This shows how great God’s grace is: as long as we truly turn to him, it is never too late.

But “I’ll believe later” has two risks. First, no one knows when they will die, and not everyone has a clear-minded chance to respond at the end. The Bible says: “Behold, now is the acceptable time. Behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Corinthians 6:2). Second, you’d miss the abundant life you could have now: peace, direction, community and the joy of walking with God.

Believing in Jesus isn’t just buying a ticket to heaven; it is beginning a relationship with God. The sooner you start, the sooner you experience his love.
qa.step: Ask yourself honestly: what is the real reason I want to wait?
qa.tip: Don’t pressure, but gently point out how precious “now” is; learn their real reason for delaying.

refs.t: He said to Jesus, “Lord, remember me when you come into your Kingdom.” Jesus said to him, “Assuredly I tell you, today you will be with me in Paradise.”
For he says, “At an acceptable time I listened to you. In a day of salvation I helped you.” Behold, now is the acceptable time. Behold, now is the day of salvation.
The thief only comes to steal, kill, and destroy. I came that they may have life, and may have it abundantly.

qa.q: Once I believe in Jesus, are there lots of things I can’t do anymore?
qa.a:
Many think believing in Jesus means a long list of “don’ts.” But the heart of faith isn’t rules; it’s relationship. Jesus said: “I came that they may have life, and may have it abundantly” (John 10:10).

Of course, life changes after believing. Some things you gradually won’t want to do—not because they’re forbidden, but because your heart has changed, like someone in love who naturally doesn’t want to hurt the other person. The Bible’s teaching is like a manual for life, showing how to live best and protecting us from harm.

Don’t fear losing out; what you gain far exceeds what you let go. And change happens step by step; you don’t have to become perfect overnight. The Holy Spirit will gently lead you.
qa.step: List the things you fear you “won’t be able to do,” and discuss with the person walking with you which are real and which are misunderstandings.
qa.tip: Avoid handing a new friend a list of rules at the start. Let them experience God’s love first; change comes from the inside out.

refs.t: The thief only comes to steal, kill, and destroy. I came that they may have life, and may have it abundantly.

“Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.”

qa.q: I work on Sundays (or need that time with family). What if I can’t go to church?
qa.a:
Many people work shifts, or Sunday is their only time with family—real difficulties. God looks at the heart, not at attendance records. Still, the Bible reminds us of “not forsaking our own assembling together” (Hebrews 10:25), because faith needs community support.

Practical options: first, find other service times (Saturday evening, weekday home groups, online gatherings). Second, Kingdom 321 Air Fellowship holds online morning readings, noon devotions and evening prayers every day—you can join anytime. Third, find time with your family, and perhaps invite them along. Fourth, set a regular time with the person walking with you to read the Bible and pray.

The key is to reserve a fixed place for God in your life. God sees your situation and will make a way for you.
qa.step: Check which meeting times your church or the online fellowship offers, and choose one to attend regularly.
qa.tip: Don’t make them feel guilty; help them find a workable spiritual rhythm.

refs.t: Let’s consider how to provoke one another to love and good works, not forsaking our own assembling together, as the custom of some is, but exhorting one another, and so much the more as you see the Day approaching.
But seek first God’s Kingdom and his righteousness; and all these things will be given to you as well.

qa.q: Can Christians drink alcohol or smoke?
qa.a:
The Bible doesn’t directly say “don’t drink,” but it clearly says, “Don’t be drunken with wine, in which is dissipation, but be filled with the Spirit” (Ephesians 5:18). So many Christians choose not to drink or to drink moderately; many Chinese churches encourage believers not to drink at all, to avoid becoming a stumbling block to themselves or others and as a witness.

The Bible doesn’t mention smoking, but we know the body is a temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:19-20), and smoking clearly harms health. Many people have quit smoking with God’s help after believing.

The more important principles: Does this glorify God? Does it harm my body? Does it control me (addiction)? Does it make others stumble? If you are struggling with addiction, don’t tough it out alone. Tell the person walking with you, and consider professional help to quit—God will be with you.
qa.step: Use two questions—“Does this glorify God? Does it control me?”—to examine one habit in your life.
qa.tip: Churches have different standards; respect your church’s teaching. Use principles rather than rules, and be alert to possible addiction.

refs.t: Don’t be drunken with wine, in which is dissipation, but be filled with the Spirit,
“All things are lawful for me,” but not all things are expedient. “All things are lawful for me,” but I will not be brought under the power of anything.

Or don’t you know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you, whom you have from God? You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. Therefore glorify God in your body and in your spirit, which are God’s.

qa.q: I’m living with my partner. What should I do now that I believe in Jesus?
qa.a:
Thank you for facing this honestly. The Bible honors marriage and sex, seeing sex as God’s good gift to a husband and wife within the covenant of marriage (Hebrews 13:4). God sets this boundary not to restrict people but to protect them: protecting the relationship, both hearts, and future families.

Believing in Jesus doesn’t mean hiding in shame; God’s grace accepts you. But going forward, God will invite you to shape this relationship his way. Some possible directions: talk openly with your partner about how faith is changing you; if you share the conviction, consider moving toward marriage; if that isn’t possible yet, consider living separately and keeping sexual boundaries before marriage.

This isn’t easy and needs wisdom and support. Please talk it through with your pastor or spiritual parent; they can walk with you step by step rather than only giving rules.
qa.step: Talk honestly with the person walking with you or your pastor about your situation.
qa.tip: Hold grace and truth together: don’t condemn, and don’t downplay. Help them make a concrete, workable decision.

refs.t: Let marriage be held in honor among all, and let the bed be undefiled; but God will judge the sexually immoral and adulterers.

Flee sexual immorality! “Every sin that a man does is outside the body,” but he who commits sexual immorality sins against his own body. Or don’t you know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you, whom you have from God? You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. Therefore glorify God in your body and in your spirit, which are God’s.

qa.q: Now that I believe, what if I have to lie at work to survive?
qa.a:
Many workplaces have gray areas: expense claims, sales figures, what you tell clients, a boss’s demands. Christians at work often face tests of honesty. The Bible says: “Therefore, putting away falsehood, speak truth each one with his neighbor, for we are members of one another” (Ephesians 4:25).

Honesty sometimes costs, but God values such a heart and often makes a way for honest people. In the Old Testament, Daniel stayed faithful and honest in a pagan court and was greatly used by God. Practical steps: do your work as well as you can without violating conscience; explain your principles to your boss with wisdom and respect; look for alternatives; discuss and pray with spiritual companions.

If some demands are clearly illegal or seriously against conscience, consider longer-term choices. God is our provider: “But seek first God’s Kingdom and his righteousness; and all these things will be given to you as well” (Matthew 6:33).
qa.step: Write down the “gray areas” you most often face at work, pray about them, and discuss them with the person walking with you.
qa.tip: Don’t reduce a complex situation to a slogan; think through workable options with them.

refs.t: Therefore, putting away falsehood, speak truth each one with his neighbor, for we are members of one another.
But seek first God’s Kingdom and his righteousness; and all these things will be given to you as well.
The integrity of the upright shall guide them, but the perverseness of the treacherous shall destroy them.

qa.q: My spouse (or future partner) doesn’t believe in Jesus. What should I do?
qa.a:
If you are already married and your spouse doesn’t believe, the Bible encourages you not to leave because of it, but to influence them with love and good conduct. Peter says believing wives can win their husbands “by the behavior of their wives without a word” (1 Peter 3:1). Don’t pressure or preach; let them see you become gentler, more considerate and more devoted to the family. Keep praying for them, and invite them to church events when the time is right.

If you aren’t married and are considering a relationship, the Bible reminds us: “Don’t be unequally yoked with unbelievers” (2 Corinthians 6:14). Marriage is life’s closest bond; differing at the core of faith creates many difficulties in values, parenting and life direction. This isn’t saying unbelievers are bad people, but is for the good of you both.

In either case, you’re welcome to talk it through with your pastor or spiritual parent.
qa.step: If married, do something especially considerate for your spouse this week; if single, write down your hopes for a future partner and bring them to God in prayer.
qa.tip: For the married, stress loving without pressure; for the single, explain biblical principles gently and give emotional support.

refs.t: In the same way, wives, be in subjection to your own husbands, so that, even if any don’t obey the Word, they may be won by the behavior of their wives without a word, seeing your pure behavior in fear.
Don’t be unequally yoked with unbelievers, for what fellowship do righteousness and iniquity have? Or what fellowship does light have with darkness?

The woman who has an unbelieving husband, and he is content to live with her, let her not leave her husband. For the unbelieving husband is sanctified in the wife, and the unbelieving wife is sanctified in the husband. Otherwise your children would be unclean, but now they are holy.

qa.q: Christians are hypocrites too. Why should I believe?
qa.a:
Sadly, some Christians’ words and actions do disappoint, and even hurt people. That is true and needs to be honestly acknowledged. But remember, the church isn’t a club for perfect people but a hospital for sinners. Jesus said: “Those who are healthy have no need for a physician, but those who are sick” (Mark 2:17).

Christians are patients being healed. Some progress quickly, some slowly, and some may not truly know Jesus yet. Refusing to see the doctor because one patient isn’t cured yet would be a shame.

Most importantly, faith focuses on Jesus, not on Christians. Jesus has never let anyone down. You can look directly at who he is, then decide whether to follow him. And you can be a different kind of Christian, so others see Jesus through you.
qa.step: Shift the focus from Christians to Jesus: read a Gospel and see what he is like.
qa.tip: Don’t defend wrong behavior; sincerely acknowledge it and apologize, and bring the focus back to Jesus.

refs.t: When Jesus heard it, he said to them, “Those who are healthy have no need for a physician, but those who are sick. I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.”
looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith, who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising its shame, and has sat down at the right hand of the throne of God.

qa.q: Does the church just want my money?
qa.a:
This concern is natural, with so many scams and stories of financial abuse. A healthy church doesn’t force people to give, and never trades giving for blessing or salvation. The Bible says: “Let each man give according as he has determined in his heart, not grudgingly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7). Seekers need feel no pressure to give at all.

Christians give out of gratitude for God’s grace, understanding that everything comes from God—to support the church’s work, the pastors’ living, and people in need. A healthy church manages its finances openly and accountably.

If you meet a group that uses giving to threaten, manipulate, or promise “give and you’ll get rich,” be cautious. Ask the person walking with you, or look at the church’s financial practices, and discern wisely.
qa.step: Observe your church: are finances transparent? Is there pressure to give? Talk about your observations with the person walking with you.
qa.tip: Tell the seeker clearly that they don’t need to give, to ease their concern.

refs.t: Let each man give according as he has determined in his heart, not grudgingly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.

But those who are determined to be rich fall into a temptation, a snare, and many foolish and harmful lusts, such as drown men in ruin and destruction. For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil. Some have been led astray from the faith in their greed, and have pierced themselves through with many sorrows.

qa.q: Do I have to go to church? Can’t I believe on my own at home?
qa.a:
Faith is personal but not individualistic. The Bible says believers are “the body of Christ, and members individually” (1 Corinthians 12:27). A finger separated from the hand can’t survive long; a believer separated from community for a long time struggles to stay spiritually healthy.

Going to church isn’t about clocking in; it’s because we need each other: to worship together, hear God’s word together, encourage, support and remind one another. A believer alone is like a single coal set aside—it soon cools; in the fire, it keeps burning.

If time, distance or past hurt makes physical church hard, start with online gatherings, a small group, or one spiritual companion. The key is: don’t walk the road of faith alone.
qa.step: This week, attend one gathering (in person or online), or meet once with a Christian friend.
qa.tip: Learn the real reason they don’t want to go (busyness? fear? past hurt?) and walk with them accordingly.

refs.t: Let’s consider how to provoke one another to love and good works, not forsaking our own assembling together, as the custom of some is, but exhorting one another, and so much the more as you see the Day approaching.
Now you are the body of Christ, and members individually.
They continued steadfastly in the apostles’ teaching and fellowship, in the breaking of bread, and prayer.

qa.q: There are so many denominations. Which one is right?
qa.a:
There are many denominations, which looks complicated. In fact, the vast majority (Presbyterian, Baptist, Free Methodist, Quaker/Friends, Methodist, Lutheran, independent churches and more) share the core faith: one God (Father, Son and Holy Spirit), Jesus as the Son of God who died and rose for us, justification by faith, and the Bible as God’s word.

Differences between denominations are mostly secondary: the mode of baptism (sprinkling or immersion), worship style, church governance, and so on. It’s like different households in one extended family, each with its own habits, but all one family.

When choosing a church, look for: the Bible as the standard, Jesus exalted, a loving community, and healthy, transparent leadership. Be especially careful of groups that claim “only we are saved,” require you to cut off family and friends, or place a person’s authority above the Bible.
qa.step: Ask the person walking with you: what denomination is our church? What are its distinctives?
qa.tip: Avoid criticizing other denominations and stress unity in Christ, while helping seekers recognize the marks of cults.

refs.t: There is one body and one Spirit, even as you also were called in one hope of your calling, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, who is over all and through all and in us all.

Beloved, don’t believe every spirit, but test the spirits, whether they are of God, because many false prophets have gone out into the world. By this you know the Spirit of God: every spirit who confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is of God, and every spirit who doesn’t confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is not of God; and this is the spirit of the Antichrist, of whom you have heard that it comes. Now it is in the world already.

qa.q: I was hurt at church and find it hard to go back. What should I do?
qa.a:
Being hurt at church often hurts more than elsewhere, because it was supposed to be the safest place. Your pain is real and deserves care. Jesus cares deeply for the wounded. He said: “Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28).

First, distinguish: it was people who hurt you, not Jesus. You can bring your hurt to Jesus first and let him heal you. As for returning to church, take your time: perhaps start with one trusted spiritual friend, or online gatherings, or look for a new, healthy church.

If the hurt involves spiritual abuse, sexual harassment, violence or financial misconduct, this isn’t a matter of “just forgive.” You have the right to speak up and seek protection and help. Forgiveness is part of healing, but forgiveness doesn’t mean silence, and it doesn’t mean returning to danger.
qa.step: Tell God honestly about the hurt you experienced, and tell one person you trust.
qa.tip: Listen first and apologize (on behalf of the church); don’t rush to urge them back or to forgive. If abuse or harm is involved, help them seek the proper channels.

refs.t: “Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.”
He heals the broken in heart, and binds up their wounds.

qa.q: I don’t know anyone at church and feel awkward. What can I do?
qa.a:
Feeling unfamiliar and awkward in a new place is normal. Many Christians felt the same the first time they went to church. The good news is that the church exists to welcome newcomers, and most churches warmly welcome them.

A few small tips: first, go with the person walking with you and ask them to introduce you to a few friends. Second, join a newcomers’ gathering or seekers’ class, where others are new too. Third, join a home group—small groups make relationships easier than big services. Fourth, give yourself time; you don’t need a close friend on day one. Attend for four to six weeks in a row, and you’ll gradually feel at home.

The Bible says we are “of the household of God” (Ephesians 2:19). Slowly you’ll find these strangers becoming family.
qa.step: At your next gathering, intentionally remember the name of one new person you meet.
qa.tip: Go to gatherings with them, introduce a few suitable brothers and sisters, and help them join a home group.

refs.t: So then you are no longer strangers and foreigners, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and of the household of God,

qa.q: My family strongly opposes my faith. What should I do?
qa.a:
Family opposition usually isn’t malicious but comes from worry: worry that you’ve been deceived, that you’ll become unfilial, that you’ll drift from the family, that no one will honor the ancestors. Understanding the worry behind it makes it easier to respond in love.

Some suggestions: First, don’t clash head-on or argue; answer “with humility and fear” (1 Peter 3:15). Second, prove it with actions: be more filial, more devoted to family and better-tempered after believing. Third, keep praying for your family—God can change hearts. Fourth, as far as your faith allows, respect your family’s feelings: always attend family gatherings, always come home for festivals. Fifth, if you are underage or financially dependent on family, discuss the best steps with a pastor.

If opposition turns into violence or threats, ensure your safety first and seek help from trusted people, the church or the relevant authorities.
qa.step: Write down why your family opposes you, consider the worry behind it, and pray for them.
qa.tip: Help them hold to faith while respecting family; don’t encourage a break with family. If there are safety concerns, address safety first.

qa.q: Will believing in Jesus make me unfilial?
qa.a:
Not at all—it should make you more filial. The first four of the Ten Commandments concern our relationship with God; the fifth is “Honor your father and mother,” the first commandment about human relationships and “the first commandment with a promise” (Ephesians 6:2). Even in his worst agony on the cross, Jesus entrusted his mother to a disciple’s care (John 19:26-27).

Christians don’t worship ancestor tablets, but they deeply value filial love: supporting parents, spending time with elders, honoring ancestors, caring for the family. Many elders became curious about Jesus precisely because they saw their believing children become more filial.

The best proof of filial love isn’t persuasion but action. One more phone call, one more visit home, one more meal with your parents—your life is the best answer.
qa.step: This week, do one concrete act of filial love for your parents or an elder.
qa.tip: Help them think of ways of showing filial love their family can feel, answering the “unfilial” worry with action.

qa.q: My friends laugh at me for being religious and say I’ve been brainwashed. It hurts.
qa.a:
Being misunderstood and laughed at really hurts. Jesus and his disciples were often mocked too. Jesus said: “Blessed are you when people reproach you, persecute you, and say all kinds of evil against you falsely, for my sake” (Matthew 5:11).

“Brainwashing” is a common worry. Real brainwashing keeps people from thinking, forbids questions, and cuts them off from the outside world. Healthy faith is the opposite: it welcomes your questions, encourages you to read the Bible and judge for yourself, and respects your family and friends. You can calmly say: “I thought it through and read for myself before believing. You’re welcome to look too.”

You don’t need to rush to convince your friends, nor distance yourself from them. Respond with sincerity, humor and without defensiveness, and keep being a good friend. Time will show that your change is real.
qa.step: Prepare a light, sincere reply you can use next time a friend teases you.
qa.tip: Comfort their emotions, and help them tell healthy faith apart from controlling groups.

qa.q: I want my family to know Jesus too. What can I do?
qa.a:
That’s a beautiful desire. Family members are the hardest to share the gospel with and the most worth it, because they know your past best. Some suggestions:

First, live it. The first gospel your family will read is your life: more gentleness, patience, filial love and responsibility will make them curious about what changed you. Second, keep praying. Pray specifically for each family member—God loves them more than you do. Third, wait for the moment. When family members face difficulty, illness or stress, show care and ask, “May I pray for you?” Fourth, invite them to relaxed events, like church festival celebrations or family activities. Fifth, share your story rather than preaching.

Jesus told a man he had healed: “Go to your house, to your friends, and tell them what great things the Lord has done for you and how he had mercy on you” (Mark 5:19). Your story is the best gospel.
qa.step: Add family members to the 920 circle on the Companion tab, and pray for one family member each day.
qa.tip: Remind them to be patient—family members often take a long time to believe. Encourage them not to give up, and not to force it.

qa.q: After believing, can I still spend time with my old friends?
qa.a:
Of course—and it matters. Jesus was called “a friend of sinners” and often ate and spent time with all kinds of people. Your friends need to see the you who now believes; they may be the people you most want to share the gospel with someday.

But be wise too. Some friend circles may make it very hard to keep your new way of life—for example, constantly pulling you into gambling, getting drunk or illegal activity. The Bible warns: “Evil companionships corrupt good morals” (1 Corinthians 15:33). Then you can adjust how you spend time together: keep being friends and keep caring, but choose healthy activities and don’t join in what would harm you.

At the same time, build new spiritual friendships at church to support you on the road of faith. You need both: spiritual friends who support you, and not-yet-believing friends you can bless.
qa.step: Think of an old friend and invite them to do something healthy and fun together, keeping the friendship going.
qa.tip: Encourage them to be salt and light rather than withdrawing from the world, while helping them build spiritual companionships.

qa.q: I’m the only Christian in my family and feel lonely.
qa.a:
Being the only believer at home is often lonely: no one to pray with, read the Bible with or go to church with, and sometimes misunderstanding to bear as well. Your feelings are real, and many have been there.

Remember, you are not alone. God promises: “I will in no way leave you, neither will I in any way forsake you” (Hebrews 13:5). And you have a spiritual family: the church, your home group, the spiritual parent walking with you, and online family in Kingdom 321 Air Fellowship. Every day’s online gatherings (morning reading, noon devotion, evening prayer) have brothers and sisters with you.

The Bible also tells of many who were “the first in their family to believe,” and later their whole household turned to God. Paul said: “Believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, and you will be saved, you and your household” (Acts 16:31). It is a promise and a hope. In your home, you may be the first lamp God has lit.
qa.step: This week, attend one online or in-person gathering, and set a regular prayer time with a spiritual companion.
qa.tip: Check in more often with the only believer in a household, and help them connect to spiritual community.

God sets the lonely in families. He brings out the prisoners with singing, but the rebellious dwell in a sun-scorched land.

qa.q: I’m not ready yet. How do I know when I’m ready to believe in Jesus?
qa.a:
Actually, no one is ever “completely ready.” If you wait until every question is answered, your life is tidied up, and you’re sure you won’t fail again, you may wait forever. When the prodigal came home he still smelled of the pigpen; the thief beside the cross had no time to do anything.

Believing in Jesus doesn’t require perfection but three things: admitting your need (I am a sinner; I can’t save myself); believing that Jesus died and rose for me; and being willing to receive him as Lord of your life. If you already agree with these three in your heart, you can begin even with some questions remaining. Questions can be worked out along the way of following him.

If you still have significant concerns, that’s okay—say them out loud and talk them through with the person walking with you. God doesn’t rush you, but he is always waiting for you.
qa.step: Write down the specific reasons you feel “not ready,” and talk them over with the person walking with you.
qa.tip: Listen for their real concerns and don’t push; if they already believe, gently invite them to pray the prayer of commitment.

qa.q: How do I know I’m really saved?
qa.a:
Assurance of salvation rests on God’s promise, not on feelings. The Bible says: “He who has the Son has the life. He who doesn’t have God’s Son doesn’t have the life. These things I have written to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, that you may know that you have eternal life” (1 John 5:12-13).

You can ask yourself: Do I admit that I am a sinner who needs Jesus? Do I believe Jesus died and rose for me? Have I received him as my Savior and Lord? If the answers are yes, God’s promise is that you have eternal life.

Besides God’s promise, there are two supporting signs: the Spirit’s witness within (Romans 8:16), letting you know in your heart that God is your Father; and gradual life change, such as a growing hunger for God’s word, sensitivity to sin, and willingness to love others. These signs grow clearer over time.
qa.step: Memorize 1 John 5:12 and say it to yourself whenever you doubt.
qa.tip: Help new believers rest assurance on God’s word rather than on emotional ups and downs.

qa.q: What do I need to reach before baptism? Do I need to know the Bible well?
qa.a:
Baptism isn’t a graduation but an enrollment. In the Bible, people were baptized as soon as they believed: on Pentecost three thousand believed and were baptized (Acts 2:41); the Ethiopian official heard the gospel and asked, “What is keeping me from being baptized?” (Acts 8:36).

Baptism doesn’t require deep Bible knowledge or great spirituality, but sincere repentance, faith in Jesus as Savior, and willingness to follow him for life. Most churches arrange a baptism class to help you understand the basics of the faith and the meaning of baptism, and an interview with the pastor to confirm your faith. It isn’t an exam but help for a good start.

After baptism the real learning begins: reading the Bible, praying, gathering, joining a home group, and growing day by day in following the Lord.
qa.step: Ask when your church’s next baptism class begins, and note it on the Journey tab.
qa.tip: Explain your church’s baptism process and ease the pressure of “not good enough,” without skipping basic understanding of the faith.

qa.q: If I sin again after baptism, is it all for nothing?
qa.a:
Baptism isn’t magic that guarantees you’ll never fail; it is a public declaration that you belong to Jesus. After baptism you will still stumble, because we are still growing. What matters is that your identity as God’s child doesn’t change when you stumble.

The Bible says: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9). When you stumble, come back to God, confess, receive forgiveness and stand up again. You don’t need to be baptized again, or doubt whether you are still a Christian.

The apostle Peter followed Jesus for three years and still denied him three times. But after the resurrection Jesus sought him out and restored him, and he became a leader of the early church. Stumbling isn’t the end; the restored become humbler and more compassionate.
qa.step: Learn to spend three minutes each night reviewing the day: confess if needed, receive forgiveness, and sleep in peace.

qa.q: My family doesn’t agree with my getting baptized. What should I do?
qa.a:
Many Chinese believers have faced this. Baptism is obedience to Jesus’ command and a public testimony, but we also value our families’ feelings. Consider these points:

First, communicate well with your family and understand why they object (worry about filial duty? about being deceived? about future ancestor rites?), and respond respectfully. Second, invite your family to your baptism so they can see what church is like. Third, give it some time; keep witnessing with filial love and a changed life—sometimes family attitudes soften. Fourth, if you are underage or financially dependent on your parents, discuss the best timing and approach with your pastor.

Whether your baptism comes sooner or later, in God’s eyes you are already his child. Keep praying; God can make a way for you and change your family’s hearts.
qa.step: With the person walking with you, write a gentle letter or a few sentences explaining to your family why you want to be baptized.
qa.tip: Assess the situation with a pastor; don’t encourage a break with family. Help them both obey the Lord and respect their family.
