qa.q: Is baptism by sprinkling or immersion? Which is right?
qa.a:
Different church traditions practice it differently. Some practice immersion (going fully under the water), picturing dying, being buried and rising with Christ (Romans 6:4); others practice sprinkling or pouring, picturing the Spirit’s cleansing and renewal. Each has biblical and historical grounds.

What matters most isn’t how much water but the faith baptism represents: repentance, faith in Jesus, union with Christ, and joining his body. Christians may practice this differently and still recognize each other as brothers and sisters in the Lord.

Be baptized according to your church’s practice, and ask your pastor to explain its meaning. At the moment of baptism, the focus is your response to Jesus, and the Father seeing you in Christ as a child he delights in.
qa.step: Ask your pastor: how does our church baptize, and what does it mean?
qa.tip: Respect different traditions and don’t criticize other churches’ practices; prepare according to your church’s practice.

qa.q: I still have doubts after believing. Does that mean my faith isn’t enough?
qa.a:
Doubt is a normal part of the journey of faith. John the Baptist doubted in prison and sent to ask Jesus, “Are you he who comes, or should we look for another?” (Matthew 11:3). Jesus didn’t rebuke him; he answered with facts and even praised him as a great prophet.

Doubt and unbelief are different. Unbelief rejects God; doubt holds questions while trusting. A father said to Jesus: “I believe. Help my unbelief!” (Mark 9:24)—an honest prayer that Jesus answered.

Facing doubt, you can: say it (don’t hide it), look for answers (read, ask), remember what God has done, and keep practicing (Bible reading, prayer, gathering). Often, faith that has passed through doubt becomes stronger than faith that never doubted.
qa.step: Write down your doubts honestly, bring them to God, and discuss them with the person walking with you.
qa.tip: Create a safe space for them to voice doubts; don’t let them feel doubt is shameful.

qa.q: I often feel unworthy. How could God love me?
qa.a:
Feeling “unworthy” often comes from past experiences: being criticized, compared, rejected, or doing wrong. We think love must be earned, that only good performance deserves it. But God’s love is completely different.

The Bible says: “But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8). God didn’t love us at our best but at our most unworthy. Grace means “undeserved, yet received.” So if you feel unworthy, it shows you understand grace.

Try putting God’s word in front of the “unworthy” voice: “you have been precious and honored in my sight, and I have loved you” (Isaiah 43:4). Your worth doesn’t come from your performance but from the one who loves you.
qa.step: Write down Isaiah 43:4 and read it aloud to yourself every morning.

qa.q: I’m afraid of being controlled or brainwashed. How can I tell?
qa.a:
That is a healthy caution. Some groups do control people in the name of religion. Healthy faith and controlling groups differ clearly.

A healthy church: uses the Bible as its standard and encourages you to read, think and ask for yourself; exalts Jesus rather than a leader; respects your family, work and personal freedom; is financially transparent; and welcomes your connections with other churches, family and friends.

Groups to be wary of: demand absolute obedience to one person; claim “only we are saved”; want you to cut off family and friends; forbid questions or other materials; control through fear or shame; demand unreasonable giving. Jesus said: “You will know the truth, and the truth will make you free” (John 8:32). True faith brings freedom, not bondage.
qa.step: Use the list above to observe the church or group you’re in contact with, and if you have concerns, discuss them with someone you trust.

qa.q: I struggle with anxiety or depression. Will believing in Jesus help? Do I still need a doctor?
qa.a:
Believing in Jesus and seeing a doctor don’t conflict. With a cold you can pray and also see a doctor and take medicine; the same is true for mental health struggles. Anxiety disorders and depression are real health conditions needing professional help, and seeking medical care doesn’t mean weak faith. God often heals through doctors, medication and counselors.

Faith can also help deeply: knowing you are loved by God, not alone, and have hope; learning to hand worries to God (Philippians 4:6-7); finding support in church community. The Psalms are full of writers honestly expressing sorrow, fear and despair, and God receives these real emotions. “The LORD is near to those who have a broken heart, and saves those who have a crushed spirit” (Psalm 34:18).

If you have thoughts of harming yourself, please contact someone you trust right away, or call your local mental health support line or emergency number. Your life is precious.
qa.step: If the struggle has lasted more than two weeks and affects daily life, make an appointment with a doctor or counselor, and tell someone you trust.
qa.tip: Encourage medical care; never say “just have enough faith.” If there is a risk of self-harm, immediately help connect them with professional resources and trusted people, and stay with them.

qa.q: My sins feel too heavy, and my past keeps haunting me.
qa.a:
Many people remain entangled with their past after believing: a wrong decision, a relationship that hurt someone, something they can’t speak of. Their minds know God has forgiven, but their hearts can’t let go.

The Bible says: “There is therefore now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1). What God has forgiven he doesn’t bring up again; he says, “I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more” (Jeremiah 31:34). If God no longer remembers, you can learn to let yourself go too.

Some help: confess it specifically to God once and receive forgiveness; if needed, apologize to or make amends with those hurt; tell a trusted mature believer and pray together, for “Confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed” (James 5:16); when the accusing voice returns, answer it with God’s word. If past trauma runs deep, consider professional counseling.
qa.step: Write Romans 8:1 on a card and read it aloud whenever the accusing voice appears.
qa.tip: Keep confidence, be gentle, don’t show shock; help them make concrete amends where needed, and suggest professional counseling for trauma.

Confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed. The insistent prayer of a righteous person is powerfully effective.

qa.q: I’m afraid of death. Can believing in Jesus help me not be afraid?
qa.a:
Fear of death is one of humanity’s deepest fears, and the Bible honestly acknowledges it. Hebrews says Jesus went through death himself to “deliver all of them who through fear of death were all their lifetime subject to bondage” (Hebrews 2:15).

Jesus rose from the dead and opened the door of death. He said: “I am the resurrection and the life. He who believes in me will still live, even if he dies” (John 11:25). For those who believe in Jesus, death isn’t the end but going home—not walking into darkness but into the Father’s embrace.

This doesn’t mean Christians won’t feel sorrow or fear facing death, but within sorrow and fear there is a greater hope. Paul could even say: “For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Philippians 1:21). When you know the ending is good, you can live today more bravely.
qa.step: Read John 14:1-3 and imagine the place Jesus is preparing for you.
qa.tip: If fear of death comes from serious illness or bereavement, be present and listen more, and gently share the hope of resurrection.

I now turn from my sin to you, and I receive Jesus as the Savior and Lord of my life. Please forgive my sins, give me new life, and let your Holy Spirit live in my heart. From today on, I want to let Jesus reign and follow him all my life. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.

bqa: Why do you want to be baptized?
Because I already believe Jesus is my Savior and Lord. Baptism obeys Jesus’ command (Matthew 28:19) and publicly declares: I belong to Jesus.
How do you know you are saved?
Not by my feelings or performance, but by God’s promise: he who has the Son has life (1 John 5:12). I have received Jesus.
Who is Jesus?
Jesus is the Son of God. He became human, died on the cross for my sins, rose on the third day, and now lives as my Lord.
What is sin?
Sin is turning from God and centering life on myself—not living as God made us—shown in thoughts, words and actions.
How are people saved?
Not by good works, but by grace through faith (Ephesians 2:8-9): repenting, believing in Jesus, and receiving him as Savior and Lord.
What does baptism represent?
That I have died, been buried and risen with Christ (Romans 6:3-4): my old self is buried, I am a new creation, and I am joined to Christ’s body—the church.
What if you sin again after baptism?
I will confess to God, who is faithful and righteous to forgive me (1 John 1:9); I will pray with spiritual companions and keep growing.
Who is the Holy Spirit?
The Holy Spirit is God, the Counselor, who lives in believers, guiding and comforting me and making me more like Jesus, bearing the fruit of the Spirit.
How will you live after baptism?
Reading the Bible and praying daily, attending gatherings and home group, letting Jesus reign, loving God and others—and one day walking with others to know Jesus.
What will you do if your family objects?
Respond with gentleness and respect, show greater filial love, keep praying for them, and witness through a changed life.
What is the Lord’s Supper?
Remembering that Jesus’ body was broken and his blood shed for me, examining myself, and hoping for his return (1 Corinthians 11:23-26).
What are the three foundations of 321?
Jesus is my example, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide.

faithbg.p: The person has no religious background and may value reason and practicality. Start from life’s meaning, the heart’s needs and verifiable clues, without assuming familiarity with religious terms.

The person comes from Chinese folk religion (temple worship, ancestor rites, praying for safety, fortune-telling, feng shui). Respect the culture and filial piety; never mock deities or ancestors. Explain the one true God and the meaning of worship, and give concrete ways to honor filial duty.

The person comes from a Buddhist or Taoist background, valuing self-cultivation, karma and serenity. Respect their pursuit of goodness and self-discipline, and gently explain grace (not by practice, but God himself coming to save) and a personal, loving God.

The person comes from a Catholic background and knows Jesus and the Bible. Start from shared faith, avoid criticizing traditions, and focus on a personal relationship with Jesus and the assurance of justification by faith.
The person has another religious background. Respect their sincere seeking; don’t belittle or attack by comparison. Clearly and gently explain who Jesus is and what is unique about the gospel.

The person has had contact with church and may have been disappointed, hurt or drifted. Listen and empathize first, distinguish human failure from Jesus himself, and invite them to know Jesus personally again.

principles: Ask about their story, their questions, their wounds first. People who feel heard can hear. “Let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak” (James 1:19).
Life first, then relationships, then ministry. Eating together, having tea and showing up when they need you matters more than a perfect Bible study.
Respect their pace; don’t rush a decision or compare their progress with others. Faith is the Spirit’s work, not your performance metric.
Focus on Jesus—not the church, not yourself, not winning arguments. Help them see who Jesus is.
Pray for them; live it yourself
Spend more time praying for them than talking with them. Your life is the first gospel they will read.
flow: Ask about life, work and family; listen to the highs and lows of their week.
Which sentence did they highlight? What did they think? Did they do the “Do” step? How did it go?
Use “See, Hear, Think, Speak, Do” on the memory verse or a Gospel passage.
Address their questions (see the Questions tab); if you don’t know, look for answers together.
Pray for their needs; invite them to pray too (one sentence is fine). Set your next meeting time.
dont: Don’t rush to correct every wrong idea.
Don’t criticize their family or former beliefs.
Don’t bombard them with church jargon (selfless, reign, overcomer…—explain in everyday words first).
Don’t promise what you can’t do, and don’t let them depend on you more than on God.
Don’t handle crises alone: for self-harm, violence, abuse or serious mental distress, connect them with a pastor and professional resources.
